Chapter one

How finding a business changed.

For twenty years, finding a business meant searching and clicking.

You typed a few words, opened tab after tab, compared reviews, and called around.

Now people just ask. And AI gives one answer.

No list of links. No tabs. One recommendation, said with confidence.

But AI can only recommend what it understands.

And for most local businesses, the facts online don't agree with each other.

Most local businesses are in pieces online.

Their hours, prices, reviews and licenses live on dozens of sites. Many of them disagree.

And now everyone is building walls.

Websites are locking AI out, charging tolls, or suing each other. Every new wall makes the answers AI gives a little worse.

  1. 2023Publishers take AI to court.The New York Times sues OpenAI and Microsoft over its articles.
  2. 2024Data goes behind deals.Reddit licenses its posts to Google and OpenAI. Most of the web gets no deal at all.
  3. 2025The web blocks AI by default.Cloudflare starts blocking AI crawlers for new sites unless they pay per crawl.
  4. 2025Stores fight shopping agents.Amazon sues Perplexity to stop its AI agent from shopping for people.

So AI guesses. Or it picks someone else.

Often the biggest name, not the best one. A great small business can be invisible without ever knowing why.

AI is deciding who to trust right now.

When everyone builds walls, the small business disappears.

How a Registry page is built.

This is where it gets nerdy. A Registry page isn't a web page with some text. It's a map of facts, built so a machine can't misread it.

Entity graphThe business, its people, services, licenses and location are each their own entity, linked to one another.
Semantic triplesEvery fact is stated as subject, relation, object. "Juniper offers lip filler." No ambiguity.
Schema and sameAsStructured data ties each entity to the same thing on the license board, maps and the web.
Provenance on every factWho said it, how we know, when it was last checked, and when it expires.
Topical mapServices, questions and answers organized the way people actually ask about them.
Machine endpointsllms.txt, sitemaps, an API and an MCP server, so agents never have to scrape.
// an AI agent asks the Registry directly
registry.find_business({ service: "lip filler", near: "Irvine, CA", open: "Saturday" })

// and gets facts it can trust, with receipts
{ "name": "Juniper Skin Studio",
  "price": { "value": 650, "stated_by": "owner", "checked": "2026-11-03" },
  "license": { "status": "active", "source": "state board" },
  "openings": ["Sat 11:00"], "book": "registry.request_booking" }

Example of the open interface we're building.

Local AI Research

We study how AI picks local businesses. Then we translate it.

Most advice about AI search is guesswork. Our research team reads the studies, checks every claim against its source and publishes what holds up, free. Then we turn it into plain-language explainers for owners, new AEO specialists and AI Consultants.

01The Journal

Original research papers. Every number cited to the study it came from, with limits stated plainly.

02Reports

What AI says about each industry and city, measured over time across ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude and Perplexity.

03Explainers

Short videos on YouTube that turn the research into what to do next, for owners, specialists and AI Consultants.

Local AI Registry Journal · Vol. 1, No. 1November 2026 · 8 min read

How Often AI Recommends Your Business: A Better Measure of Local Visibility

Local AI Registry Research · 14 references · 9 peer-reviewed

Abstract. A single AI answer is an observation, not a ranking. Across studies of web search, generative search, local audits and medical recommendations, answers to the same question vary from run to run, by place, by wording and over time. We argue that local visibility is best measured as a recommendation frequency under stated conditions, and propose five principles for measuring it.
Five principles for measuring AI visibility
  1. Report a rate, with its conditions
  2. Sample enough answers
  3. Separate being named from being first
  4. Verify what is counted
  5. Tell noise from real change

Founder's story

I opened my own med spa, and I got taken for a ride. Agencies promised the world, locked me into long contracts and sent reports I couldn't verify. Their case studies were cherry-picked, and when the results didn't come, nobody was accountable. I spent twenty years in search at Google and Microsoft, and I still couldn't tell what was real. If I couldn't, how could any other owner? So we built the opposite: one record you own, public track records, no long contracts, and a guarantee.

We already help all kinds of local businesses. The road is where we go all in, one industry at a time: the research, the specialists, the AI Consultants and the proof. Each stop is picked for one reason: AI matters more there than anywhere else.

At every stop we start with the best in the vertical: the key opinion leaders, influencers and practice leaders other owners follow. When they trust the Registry, their industry pays attention.
